newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Labour woes said scaring industry from Cambodia.
newsitem.headline: Labour woes said scaring industry from Cambodia.

text.p: The head of the Cambodian Garment Manufacturers' Association said on Tuesday that continued labour unrest is driving away investors and could spur the collapse of the local garment industry.
"This is having a tremendous impact on the industry. It's going to be very bad...the garment industry here could collapse," Van Sou Ieng told Reuters in a telephone interview.
His comments came as about 300 garment workers led the fourth protest in 10 days in Phnom Penh.
"At least two factories are already thinking of closing and leaving Cambodia," he added, declining to name them.
Van Sou Ieng, who heads Wing Tai Apparel, represents most of the 34 garment factories in Cambodia, which together employ more than 16,000 workers.

The garment industry is one of the country's fastest growing industrial sectors, but in the past ten days it has been plagued by protests from workers, who say they are underpaid, overworked and mistreated.
On Tuesday, workers from Gennon Cambodia Garment Manufacturing Ltd went on strike and marched through the capital to protest their working conditions and demand more pay.
The protest was led by leaders of a newly formed trade union under the stewardship of opposition leader Sam Rainsy.
Lee Fung Tai, director of Gennon, said he would meet with Sam Rainsy, head of the Khmer Nation Party, and workers on Wednesday to discuss their grievances.

Last week, more than 3,000 workers from Cambodia Garments Ltd (CGL) held three protests, capped by a march on the National Assembly. They later announced they had won pay raises, maternity leave, sick leave and a 47-hour work week.
CGL is owned by Malaysia's Raylee Readywear Sdn Bhd.
Van Sou Ieng said the demonstrations were destructive.

"Over this incident, we had a deluge of calls questioning the wisdom of doing future business in Cambodia," he said in a statement. "European buyers of garments are watching and perhaps already deciding to channel some business originally meant for Cambodia to other, more reliable sources."
He said since the industry was in its early stage it was easy for investors to pull out and that wage concessions could make Cambodia too expensive for business.
